title: Natasha Hunt on PWR, Gloucester-Hartpury upheaval and the Lions: ‘It would be the cherry on top of the cake’
article_text:
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Returning from Red Roses camp to prepare for a new Premiership Women’s Rugby (PWR) season, Natasha ‘Mo’ Hunt was hit by the realisation of how much had changed. For the first time in three campaigns, Gloucester-Hartpury enter not as defending champions but as challengers; Saracens, the league’s first dynastic power, were restored to their throne in June with a final demolition job against the upstart Trailfinders. A relinquishing of their crown precipitated a summer of drastic change – gone from an environment known colloquially known as “The Circus” are, among others, Zoe Stratford, Tatyana Heard, Sarah Beckett, Sisilia Tuipulotu, Bethan Lewis and Kelsey Jones.

Or, as ringmaster Hunt puts it: “Pretty much my friendship group has all gone.” New mother Stratford (nee Aldcroft) was her business partner and co-captain; having lost charismatic coach Sean Lynn to Wales last year, there is certainly a different feel about the place.

“Personally, it does feel like a huge change,” Hunt admits. “It will take some getting used to. I’m so unbelievably chuffed for Zo in her next chapter, but I’m gutted that I don’t get to pull on the shirt again with her in the changing room. She is an unbelievable athlete and human to be around.”

But out of upheaval can come opportunity. The outstanding France centre Gabrielle Vernier is an eye-catching arrival in the West Country, and Hunt is confident she and her squad can retain a unique culture built around the person as much as the player. “You get the best out of people when you know what makes them tick and on a deeper level,” she explains. “That’s something we’ve driven at Gloucester.

“It’s not something we’ve ever spent loads and loads of time on. It needs to be organic to have a good culture. We were really pro on recruiting good people. If someone was to come in, they had to be a good human and add to the environment. The forward pack I had in front of me was just insane for three years, but it was also about the humans they were off the pitch. It is about enjoying your time together. With the Red Roses and Gloucester-Hartpury, I’ve been lucky that I’ve been part of two teams with that unbelievable culture and unbelievable athletes who are really driven to push. Have high standards, but also be a bit silly with each other.”

Those high standards met new challenges in a fascinating season last time around. Though Gloucester-Hartpury topped the table, their semi-final defeat to Trailfinders came as little surprise given how things had coalesced in Ealing during the course of the campaign. If few would have forecast Bristol as eight-placed finishers, the Bears finished with just one win fewer than the beaten finalists – and have brought in Ellie Kildunne to supercharge their revival following a somewhat messy exit from Harlequins.

A reshaping of the league perhaps looms with Irish, Welsh and Scottish interest in fielding teams in the future, and the Rugby Football Union (RFU) courting American investment, but, for now, the scramble for play-off places could be more competitive than ever. Tighthead prop Tuipulotu has pitched up at Quins, where she is joined by Marlie Packer and Rosie Galligan – two more new parents after the pair welcomed a daughter in October.

Stratford – once back from maternity leave – Heard and Beckett could turn Sale Sharks into contenders; Loughborough have added a Canadian core; and even Leicester, of which there were real concerns last year, have lured Wallaroos whizz-kid Caitlyn Halse to Welford Road. And that’s without mentioning Exeter, with a squad as complete as any.

There may be an added significance to this season, too. The first Women’s British and Irish Lions squad will be named in mid-May just before the PWR season resumes following the Six Nations; with virtually all of those hoping to figure in Jo Yapp’s selection plying their trade in England, and club contests sometimes offering a better gauge than at Test level given the Red Roses’ dominance, the battle for places could be fierce.

“I’ve been lucky enough to be involved in two Team GB squads, and having all of those different cultures is great,” Hunt says. “If anyone says they aren’t thinking about it, they are lying, because it is such a huge opportunity as individuals but for the women’s game as well. I hate talking about it. What will be will be. The only thing that I can control is how I play.”

It is more than 15 years now since the scrum half made her international debut. For a player who contemplated retirement after her omission from England’s World Cup squad in 2022, the Lions is a pretty significant carrot for keeping going – and a dedicated character, who gave up alcohol for a year before the Red Roses’ triumph on home soil, has a drive to get there.

“Sometimes people get stuck into your age but I want to flip the narrative on it. I’m 37 now and that should be celebrated. I was capped in 2011; I’ve been doing this a hell of a long time now.

“I want to go out still on the top of my game. If you can still perform to the level required, I don’t think age should ever be a consideration when picking someone. [The Lions] is a reason for still playing. It was part of the decision-making to keep going and see if that is something I could potentially achieve. But at the same time, I’m so content with my career. It won’t define me and my rugby. It would just be the cherry on top of the cake.”

title: Wales show they have bench impact in All Blacks win
article_text:
They say rugby is now a game that relies on 23 players.

There was ample evidence of that during Wales' remarkable 35-28 win against New Zealand last Saturday.

The headline acts were the 346 tackles made by the team, which was a world record for an international match.

The 38 tackles managed by lock Dafydd Jenkins matched the top individual tally, while Jac Morgan (31), James Botham (30), Eddie James (25), captain Dewi Lake (24) and Max Llewellyn (23) were not far behind.

It was the impact of the bench that also proved crucial in the defensive stand of the final quarter.

Replacement back rower Taine Plumtree popped up with two crucial turnovers, while Gareth Thomas and Ben Carter made a combined 32 tackles in 42 minutes.

Ospreys prop Thomas managed 19 in 26 minutes, while lock Carter's return was 13 in 16 minutes to add to the remarkable statistics and contributions.

Thomas has been Wales' third-choice loose-head in recent times behind Nicky Smith and Rhys Carre.

He found himself promoted to the bench last Saturday, with Smith starting and Carre left out of the squad.

Thomas responded by providing one of the most impressive replacement defensive displays in living memory, especially for a prop.

"I have not made as many tackles in such a short space of time," said Thomas.

"But I kept looking up and they were running at me! It was a wild last 20 minutes, but every single person on the pitch was doing their job.

"Everybody was doing what they could, emptying every little bit of energy they had to stop them from scoring."

Alongside his tackles, he also held All Blacks number eight Wallace Sititi over the line, one of three vital interventions of its kind, with Botham, Morgan and fly-half Dan Edwards also involved in the efforts that denied New Zealand.

"It was a sketchy moment because there was a lot of space there," said Thomas.

"I knew if I went to hit him hard it could have been a try, easily so I kind of soaked him up over the line.

"It's something we've been working with, a last resort that Peter Murchie and Dan Lydiate [Wales defence coaches] have brought in.

"It was nice that transfered to the game. Straight after you're thinking what's my next job and don't think about it.

"But after the game I've had that video sent to me 50 to 100 times on social media. I've watched it a few times and it's a big moment."

Thomas, 33, is one of the elder statesmen in the group.

"It's a very special feeling," said Thomas.

"I was sat in bed the other night, just watching the videos of reactions in pubs and places around Wales. I love it how it made everyone feel, what it meant to people.

"I had a message saying how special it made their 92-year-old friend and he's happy to go to the grave now after that. So special to make people feel like that.

"We can't stop watching the reactions because it makes you feel like a fan.

"I would love to have been a fan watching it, it shows what it means to see ex-players with tears in their eyes."

Dragons co-captain Carter, 25, was dropped to being a replacement following the 28-21 win against Japan, with Adam Beard coming into start alongside Jenkins.

Beard made his own telling contribution in an improved Wales line-out and racked up 21 tackles in 64 minutes before Carter came onto help finish the job.

"I probably would have liked to have spent a bit more time with the ball and maybe a bit further up the field," said Carter.

"I do enjoy the defensive aspect of the game, so it was brilliant.

"They were coming at us very direct and it always felt good in those defensive sets and we were pleased.

"I was tired and I can't imagine how the boys were feeling that they had already played 60 minutes.

"There were some big shifts and tackle numbers from a lot of the boys.

"The biggest thing was you could feel the the fight for each other on the pitch, and the supporters could see it as well."

Carter, who has played 23 internationals, hopes to be involved this weekend against Australia, while Beard is suffering from a sore shoulder.

"There's a lot of belief in this group anyway and they believe that's the sort of performance we can put in," said Carter.

"Just to live it and to get that result will only help our confidence.

"There is probably a bit of expectation on us now, and the group looks forward to carrying that into these next games."

title: The Youth Olympic medallists set for Global Youth 7s in Auckland
article_text:
Rugby Australia has unveiled the Australia Under 18 Girls and Australian Schoolgirls squads for this year’s Global Youth 7s in Auckland, with 10 medallists from the Dakar Youth Olympics set to participate in the prestigious age-grade event.

Queensland Reds prospect Aimee Henry captained Australia at the Youth Olympics, with the talented squad making it through to the gold medal match. But the Aussies fell just short of gold in an extra-time thriller against Kenya, who claimed a 17-12 win in the Senegal capital.

Henry and nine other sevens representatives from those Games will again get the chance to wear green and gold on the world stage, with RA naming 26 players across two squads to play across the ditch on December 18 to 20.

Dakar silver medallists Grace Buchanan, Keira Callaghan, TJ Murray, Layne Prince, Cobi Ryan-Last and Darci Turinui have been selected in the U18 Girls squad. Another three silver medallists have been named in the Australian Schoolgirls side.

90 per cent of those in the full-time Australia Sevens program played at Global Youth 7s during their rise through the ranks, including prolific try-scorers Maddison Levi and Faith Nathan, and captain Isabella Nasser.

The invitational tournament brings together future stars of the HSBC SVNS Series, with some of the world’s best emerging sevens talent taking the field. Mitch Bebb and Asako Ono will coach the U18 side, who claimed titles in 2018, 2019 and 2023.

“The Global Youth 7s is an incredibly important part of our pathway,” Rugby Australia Women’s Sevens National Talent Pathways Manager Lachlan Parkinson said.

“It provides our emerging athletes with the opportunity to experience international competition, test themselves against some of the best young talent in the world and understand what it takes to compete at the next level.

“Just as importantly, it allows us to continue building depth within Australian Rugby Sevens and creating a sustainable pathway for the next generation of athletes coming through.

“Both squads have an exciting mix of talent and potential, and we believe both teams have the ability to compete very well at this tournament.”

Australia U18 Schoolgirls Head Coach Luke Zeremes added: “This is the fourth consecutive year that an Australian Schoolgirls Rugby Sevens team has been selected, and it’s exciting to see the continued growth and development of the program.

“We have players representing New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria and Western Australia in 2026, which highlights the depth of emerging talent across the country.

“The Global Youth Sevens in Auckland is a fantastic opportunity for these young athletes to test themselves against quality international opposition, with a mix of national development programs and invitational teams from New Zealand, Australia and beyond.

“It’s an exciting tournament that will challenge the players both individually and collectively, while providing invaluable experiences and opportunities to continue their development.”

title: Black Ferns Sevens icons return in 18-player squad for SVNS Series
article_text:
Michaela Brake, Sarah Hirini and Shiray Kaka are back in black for the 2026/27 HSBC SVNS Series, with the Olympic gold medallists named in an 18-player Black Ferns Sevens squad. Coach Cory Sweeney has also selected three uncapped players in the group.

Brake, Hirini and Kaka all became first-time mothers over the last 18 months, and are now juggling having young families with the demands of elite sport. Social media sensation Kaka documented this journey with the ‘Back to Black’ series.

The experienced trio are joined in the lineup by uncapped players Kavanah Lene, Le-Oxeayn Maiu’u and Renee Holmes. Holmes starred as the Black Ferns won the postponed 2021 Rugby World Cup on home soil, and was a regular starter during last year’s event as well.

Holmes recently described Black Ferns Sevens and Black Ferns teammate Jorja Miller as “an absolute freak” in an interview with RugbyPass, after the two had shared the field in recent SVNS warm-up events both at home and abroad.

Miller, who is a two-time World Rugby Sevens Player of the Year, has retained the vice-captaincy, as confirmed by New Zealand Sevens on Tuesday. Risaleaana Pouri-Lane will continue to lead the side, taking on captaincy duties full-time last season.

Maia Davis, Jazmin Felix-Hotham, Jaymie Kolose, Danii Mafoe, Manaia Nuku, Mahina Paul, Alena Saili, Kelsey Teneti, Katelyn Vahaakolo and Olive Watherston have also been named to represent the Black Ferns Sevens this season.

“It’s been great to see the energy of the new players in the squad alongside the leadership of our more experienced core,” Sweeney said.

“It has been a very competitive preseason with players pushing for places and that’s a positive sign as we look toward the start of the HSBC SVNS Series.”

The Black Ferns Sevens dominated the SVNS Series regular season in 2025/26, winning five of six events. But the New Zealanders fell just short in the World Championship race, with arch-rivals Australia taking out titles in Valladolid and Bordeaux.

title: Olympic medallist returns to All Blacks Sevens on loan from Chiefs
article_text:
Tokyo Olympics silver medallist Andrew Knewstubb has returned to the All Blacks Sevens on loan from the Chiefs, with the Willie Rickards-coached squad also featuring a handful of uncapped players for the 2026/27 HSBC SVNS Series season.

Knewstubb has helped Canterbury win back-to-back provincial titles and is coming off a maiden Super Rugby Pacific campaign with the Highlanders. The first five-eighth recently moved up north, selected by the Chiefs in the wider training group draft.

But the Chiefs have loaned Knewstubb out to the All Blacks Sevens, just as the Hurricanes have done with Waisake Salabiau. Salabiau is one of five uncapped prospects in the 22-man squad, along with Grady Forbes, Adam Morrison, Brayden Neilson and Nathan Salmon.

Salmon is coming off a historic season with Northland, with the Taniwha ending their long-lasting Ranfurly Shield drought en route to the final. The winger also spent time Stateside with the New England Free Jacks during the 2026 Major League Rugby season.

Brothers Rob and Brady Rush are in the All Blacks Sevens fold, also looking to build on an unforgettable NPC campaign with Northland. Rob was named Player of the Match after the Shield win over Canterbury in Christchurch.

Rob Rush will help lead the side this season, with New Zealand Sevens announcing the captains on Wednesday. Rush and experienced campaigner Sione Molia have been named co-captains, while former skipper Tone Ng Shiu also brings experience to the squad.

Joe Webber has been included, with coach Willie Rickards bringing the five-time World Series [SVNS Series] champion back.

Sam Clarke, Jayden Keelan, Kele Lasaqa, Michael Manson, Ngarohi McGarvey-Black, Fletcher Morgan, Sofai Notoa-Tipo, Akuila Rokolsioa, Bradley Tocker and Riley Williams round out the group.

“Our group has come together really well through the preseason and our leaders have set a great example for the new players coming into the environment,” Rickards said.

“There’s a sense of excitement about the season and some young players who are ready to make their mark.”

The All Blacks Sevens will announce a 13-player travelling squad for the Dubai and Cape Town Sevens on Friday, November 20.

title: Olympic Solidarity support helps rugby sevens teams make history at Dakar 2026
article_text:
The first Olympic sporting event to be held on African soil provided a memorable stage for rugby sevens, with developing rugby nations making their mark and young athletes showcasing the growing strength of the game across the continent.

Among the standout achievements were Kenya's historic gold medal in the women's competition and Madagascar's bronze, with both teams having participated in an Olympic Solidarity-supported training camp in Tunisia just weeks before stepping onto the podium in Dakar.

Organised by World Rugby in October in collaboration with the International Olympic Committee, the camp provided an important opportunity for both teams to fine-tune their preparations ahead of the Youth Olympic Games, combining on-field training with educational sessions covering anti-doping, safeguarding and the Olympic values.

The initiative reflected the wider objectives of Olympic Solidarity, which supports athletes and National Olympic Committees around the world, helping to strengthen sporting development and create opportunities for young athletes to compete on the international stage.

For Kenya and Madagascar, that support formed part of a journey that culminated in unforgettable moments in Dakar. Kenya's Rising Lionesses claimed gold in dramatic fashion, defeating Australia 17-12 in extra time, with Mitchelle Chemtai scoring the decisive try to secure the country's first Olympic rugby sevens gold medal. The victory also marked the first time an African nation had won rugby sevens gold at either the Olympic Games or Youth Olympic Games.

Madagascar, meanwhile, celebrated a milestone of its own, defeating Czechia 26-10 to secure bronze and claim the nation's first-ever Olympic medal in any sport.

Reflecting on Kenya's achievement, Kenya Rugby Union CEO Thomas Odundo highlighted the importance of the support received throughout the team's development. “I'm very proud of the girls. What started as developing the national sports system was then followed by this training camp and finally materialised into a medal. That's just amazing.”

The success of both teams underlined the importance of sustained investment in emerging rugby nations, with initiatives such as the Olympic Solidarity-supported camp helping to provide young athletes with the preparation, knowledge and experience needed to perform at the highest level.

World Rugby CEO Alan Gilpin, who attended the Games in Dakar, witnessed the historic achievements and the enthusiasm surrounding rugby sevens at Africa's first Youth Olympic Games. “Dakar 2026 was a special moment for rugby and for the growth of the game in Africa. Seeing Kenya and Madagascar make history on the Olympic stage was incredibly inspiring and demonstrated the talent and potential that exists across the continent.

“Through our collaboration with Olympic Solidarity, we can help provide young players and emerging rugby nations with opportunities to develop, prepare and compete. The achievements in Dakar are a wonderful example of what that support can help make possible, and we look forward to building on this momentum.”

The rugby sevens competition produced memorable performances across both tournaments, with France securing men's gold ahead of South Africa and Argentina, while Kenya topped the women's podium ahead of Australia and Madagascar.

Beyond the medals, Dakar 2026 demonstrated the opportunities that rugby sevens can create for young athletes around the world, and the important role that collaboration and targeted development initiatives can play in helping more countries realise their potential on the Olympic stage.

title: England's Atkinson set for All Blacks dream date
article_text:
England centre Seb Atkinson says he is living a childhood dream as he prepares to face New Zealand in Twickenham on Saturday.

The Gloucester pivot has recovered from a hip knock and is set to return to the starting XV at number 12 for the visit of the wounded All Blacks.

For Atkinson, this weekend's game comes a fortnight after he made his first Allianz Stadium appearance with England in the 45-22 thumping of Australia.

"It's sort of ticking off wishes and dreams that you have as a young aspiring rugby player," Atkinson told BBC Sport.

"Watching [England against New Zealand in 2012] when Manu [Tuilagi] scored that try and set up that try, the big performance in the semi-final of the World Cup a few years ago [in 2019].

"And obviously I was frustrated to not be available last year when the team put in a good performance.

"So a lot of things spring to mind and to be able to be out there and show what I can do on that stage will be really exciting for me personally."

New Zealand - beaten 33-19 by England on the same stage last November - will recall several big-name players this weekend.

They are looking to make amends for a shock defeat by Wales in Cardiff, with Atkinson set to line up against the heralded Jordie Barrett in midfield.

Atkinson has observed and admired Barrett at his best, but he is determined to be his own man.

"I love rugby and I love watching rugby and I love watching the likes of Jordie and [South Africa World Cup winner] Damian de Allende and try and take bits from their game," Atkinson said.

"But I know that fundamentally for me to get better as a player I need to be myself. I can't just replicate other people.

"You're trying to take away what they're good at - but also show what you're good at too."

New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie said his group would "poke each other in the chest" at the start of this week as they pick the bones out of a chastening first loss to Wales in 73 years.

Rennie said the All Blacks "let the country down" against the Welsh, but with an expected 500 caps of experience to come into the New Zealand matchday squad, England senior coach Richard Wigglesworth says the home side are preparing for the highest standard of opposition regardless of what happened in Cardiff.

"It changes nothing," Wigglesworth said.

"We get a different team. It is a massive challenge for us. England against New Zealand is an historic game. We just want to bring the best of us and give it a good rip."

title: Shaun Edwards to save England? What all 5 teams require to reach the Nations Championship final
article_text:
Shaun Edwards to save England? What all 5 teams require to reach the Nations Championship final

Five teams enter the sixth and final round of the Nations Championship on Saturday still capable of reaching next weekend’s inaugural final at Twickenham’s Allianz Stadium – and four of them will be playing one another.

France, England and Ireland remain alive in the northern conference, while New Zealand and South Africa are the only survivors in the south. France lead on 21 points, one ahead of England and Ireland, while the All Blacks hold the same one-point advantage over the Springboks.

That makes Saturday particularly intriguing. England host New Zealand at 14:10 before Ireland face South Africa at 16:40, meaning both matches directly influence the race on either side of the equator. An England win would strengthen their own final hopes while simultaneously opening the door for South Africa; an Irish victory later would do the same for Ireland while damaging the Springboks.

A buoyant France, off the back of their 21-19 win over the Springboks, are the exception. They face an Argentina side in Paris already eliminated from final contention at 20:10 and will kick off knowing precisely what England and Ireland have done.

The equation is simplest for Les Bleus. A bonus-point victory guarantees top spot, taking Fabien Galthié’s side beyond anything England or Ireland can reach.

A four-point victory, however, could leave the door open. A bonus-point win for England or Ireland would take either side level with France on 25 points and five victories.

That would make points difference decisive. The competition’s tiebreakers are, in order: most wins, points difference, tries difference, most tries scored and, remarkably, a coin toss if the teams still cannot be separated.

England have positioned themselves particularly well for that possibility. Their 73-8 demolition of Fiji in July and their recent 78-15 victory over Japan have helped build a +134 points difference, which is 54 better than France’s +80 and 77 clear of Ireland’s +57 with a round to play.

Steve Borthwick’s side therefore have an enviable cushion if they can overcome New Zealand. This is, however, perhaps the hardest match to call of the weekend, or at least for teams vying for the final.

England have indeed shown an uptick in form and performances in November, and will also take encouragement from their 33-19 victory over the All Blacks at Allianz Stadium last November. But they will be up against a side surely looking to respond emphatically to their 35-28 defeat to Wales at the weekend – their first loss to the Welsh in 73 years.

But even victory at 14:10 will leave England facing a nervous wait of almost six hours before France kick off.

While he may not be part of the England coaching set-up, Argentina defence coach Shaun Edwards could do Borthwick a huge favour by orchestrating a defensive masterclass to prevent the free-scoring French from amassing four tries.

Ireland’s path is less forgiving. They need to beat South Africa and hope France leave points behind against Argentina, while what England have already achieved will also shape their target. Andy Farrell’s side have won four of their last six meetings with the world champions, although South Africa won 24-13 in Dublin last year in a savage display of the scrummaging prowess.

France, meanwhile, have won six of their last seven against Argentina, but, curiously, have only managed a four-try bonus point in one of their last meetings with the Pumas.

The southern race could be settled much earlier.

New Zealand sit on 22 points to South Africa’s 21, so a bonus-point win over England would guarantee the All Blacks top spot before Rassie Erasmus’ side even take the field.

Anything less gives the Springboks an opportunity, and they will know exactly what is required when they kick off in Dublin. South Africa need to collect two more competition points than New Zealand to move ahead outright, while finishing level could bring the tiebreakers into play.

Again, the Boks have built themselves a huge advantage. Their 66-7 demolition of Italy has contributed to a +138 points difference, compared with New Zealand’s +66.

South Africa need to collect two more competition points than New Zealand to move ahead outright, while collecting one more would leave the two level and bring the tiebreakers into play.

There is therefore the potential for one result to reverberate through both conferences. England beating New Zealand could simultaneously put Borthwick’s side on course for the final and hand the initiative to South Africa, while an Ireland win over the Boks could enhance their own hopes and shut the door on Erasmus.

And after all that, France will have the final say.

The two conference winners meet in the Nations Championship final at Allianz Stadium on Sunday, November 29, with every other nation paired against the team finishing in the corresponding position in the opposite conference during finals weekend.

title: Ben Earl backs surprise location to host 2028 Nations Championship finals weekend
article_text:
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The England rugby No 8 Ben Earl believes the next finals weekend of rugby’s Nations Championship should be held away from a traditional stronghold of the sport, floating Las Vegas and Brazil as possible candidates for the showpiece event.

Twickenham’s Allianz Stadium will host the inaugural finals next weekend, with six games held across three days based on pool placings across the July and November international windows.

England are vying with France and Ireland to top the northern hemisphere pool, while New Zealand and South Africa are assured of top-two finishes in the southern hemisphere group.

Earl had been a critic of the new competition during England’s demanding itinerary earlier in the year, with Steve Borthwick’s side playing Tests in Johannesburg, Liverpool and Santiago del Estero across consecutive Saturdays in July.

But the 28-year-old has come around on the format, and believes it offers a good opportunity to grow the game.

“I feel like it's taking shape nicely now,” Earl said. “I don't want to say I was wrong because that's not my style. But you can see the method in it now. The summer obviously needs a tweak in whatever way that looks like.

“There's some big games this weekend. Hopefully for the fans, they've enjoyed it. We certainly enjoyed playing in it. And obviously, it's a bit nicer being at home.”

France and Spain are understood to have registered interest in hosting the finals weekend in the future, while Rugby Football Union (RFU) chief executive Bill Sweeney also indicated that Twickenham would be willing to hold the event again.

It had been mooted that Qatar would be the venue for the 2028 edition, though that is thought to be off the table after a sponsorship deal with Qatar Airways fell through amid the conflict in the Middle East.

A number of top Tests will be held in the United States, though, over the next half-decade as World Rugby builds up to the 2031 Rugby World Cup, and Earl believes “Sin City” would be an ideal fit.

“You'd be hard pressed not to say Vegas, wouldn't you? That would be a good fun,” Earl admitted.

“People in Brazil apparently love the game. What about something cool like that? Like, I don't know, take it somewhere where there's tier two nations. And we all get a chance to go somewhere new that we haven't been before, because we're all in the entertainment industry at the end of the day. Let's try and grow the game.

“We know if we go to London, we know if we go to wherever, people are going to turn up and watch because people love it. But let's go somewhere cool, like a Hong Kong or a Spain.

“There's obvious places that we didn't get a chance to go to that would be cool.”

England face New Zealand in their final pool fixture on Saturday afternoon.

title: Scotland coach insists door remains open for Blyth-Lafferty to make World Cup
article_text:
The door remains open for Ollie Blyth-Lafferty to stake a claim for Scotland’s Rugby World Cup squad despite the young tighthead being omitted from the squad for the Nations Championship clash with Japan.

That is the view of assistant coach Pieter de Villiers, despite the Edinburgh youngster being released from the Scotland squad ahead of Saturday's game at Murrayfield.

Blyth-Lafferty was initially left out of Gregor Townsend’s squad for the autumn before being drafted in alongside his club-mate D’arcy Rae when Elliot Millar Mills was ruled out injured.

It was no surprise the 20-year-old was not thrown in against New Zealand or Australia but a game against a struggling Japan side presented an opportunity to test his ability at international level.

However, Scotland have decided to stick with established first choice Zander Fagerson plus Rae and Will Hurd for this weekend's game.

De Villiers, who won 69 caps as a tighthead prop in his own Test career, explained the decision to release Blyth-Lafferty, known as OBL, when he addressed the media on Tuesday afternoon.

"We're fortunate to have a good bit of tighthead depth at the moment," he said.

"When Elliot Millar Mills got injured, D’arcy Rae was the next tighthead in. But D’arcy was also just coming back from injury as well and we thought it was a brilliant opportunity for OBL as a young tighthead to come in as well and to just be with the group and grow with the group and measure himself against the international props as well.

"But D’arcy was always the next guy in. So as soon as he was 100 per cent fit to go, then normally we only keep three tightheads in the group.

"It was good to have OBL in and him getting exposure at club level often is good. Him training and scrummaging against the international props also gives him an idea to see where he is and where he still needs to grow as a young prop, which is only normal. So I think he's doing really well in his progress in becoming an international prop.

“But at the age of 20 as well, certain things will take a bit of time to settle and grow. So we're very happy with his progress, definitely.”

But the former France prop insisted the door remains open for Blyth-Lafferty to force his way into the picture next year ahead of the Rugby World Cup.

"There's definitely a chance for him," he said.

"He's done so well as a young tighthead to play professional club rugby and really scrummage well.

"The international level is a level up again and you also want to make sure that you put a young player in the best possible conditions for him to thrive. We tend to think that what we have done here in terms of exposing him is the best way. Getting more club rugby under the belt as well.

"This period from now onwards until the Six Nations will again be telling in terms of his growth and then we'll take it from there once the Six Nations come and we'll see how we go."

There have been comparisons made between Blyth-Lafferty and current first choice Zander Fagerson, who made his Scotland debut as 20-year-old a decade ago.

"He's done really well for us through this campaign," he said.

"As much as we've spoken about a couple of scrum frustrations that there were he's been consistent outside of set piece as well. He's been carrying well again.

"He's been training well. He's had a couple of niggles injury wise at the back end of last season which he's overcome. I think he's in great shape in terms of core conditioning and he's in great shape mentally as well.

"He's been strong for the group coming into this campaign and it's great to see him in great form."

title: Rassie Erasmus set to miss 2027 Rugby World Cup group stage - Sports & Betting News
article_text:
Shockwaves have been sent across international rugby union, as World Rugby announce a six-game suspension for South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus.

The defending world champions fell to a rare defeat in Paris in round five of the 2026 Nations Championship leading to a bizarre rant from their head coach, accusing the referee and governing body of numerous wrongdoings.

In his post-match press conference on the Monday, which followed the defeat to France, Erasmus was as quoted saying "Is that not match fixing?! Is that not interfering with the outcome?" when referencing a number of so-called 'hip-drop' tackles which he believed were missed by the officials.

The ruling, which the back-to-back Rugby World Cup winners have already confirmed they have "requested a full hearing" to appeal, is set to have extreme ramifications for the Springboks and the whole of international rugby, with the showcase tournament just around the corner.

Should the suspension stand, the Springboks are set to be without their talismanic head coach - who has been in charge for both the 2019 and 2023 World Cup triumphs - for the start of the 2027 tournament.

On Tuesday evening, World Rugby announced that they had placed an automatic six-match suspension on South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus.

Two of those matches will be served in the remainder of the Autumn, with the other four set to be in 2027.

While South Africa's full 2027 Rugby World Cup warm up schedule may not have been released, as things stand, Rassie Erasmus would miss all three of South Africa's group stage matches.

Despite this, it is likely that the Springboks will confirm more World Cup warm-ups in due course, though it's unclear whether or not those would count towards Erasmus' suspension.

As things stand, Rassie Erasmus would return to the Springboks' hotseat for the Rugby World Cup round of 16, which gets underway on the weekend of the 23rd and 24th October 2027.

title: Rassie Erasmus: South Africa head coach banned for six matches
article_text:
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has been banned for six matches by World Rugby over comments he made about match officials in his side's Nations Championship defeat by France last week.

Speaking at a news conference conference in Dublin on Monday before the Springboks' match with Ireland, Erasmus questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: "is that not match-fixing?".

The two-time Rugby World Cup-winning coach was referencing the implementation of new rules surrounding hip-drop and knee-drop tackles, and felt the laws were not being applied correctly.

It comes after Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast became the first player to be cited for a hip-drop tackle in Ireland's win over Fiji on Saturday, which was not penalised in-play by referee Angus Gardner and television match official [TMO] Mike Adamson.

World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments "suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match".

In response, South Africa Rugby said it has requested a full misconduct hearing and an opportunity for Erasmus to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".

It is the third time Erasmus has been sanctioned by World Rugby over his comments about match officials.

When he was South Africa's director of rugby, he was suspended for two months by World Rugby after he posted an hour-long video criticising the refereeing in the Springboks' opening Test defeat by the British and Irish Lions in 2021.

World Rugby found the video contained "multiple abusive and insulting comments and attacks on the officials".

In 2022, he received a two-match ban for a series of tweets criticising officials in a defeat by France.

Erasmus' latest ban has been imposed under World Rugby's match official abuse sanction process, which was introduced by the governing body in July.

If the suspension is upheld, Erasmus will miss Saturday's game with Ireland in Dublin (16:40 GMT), next week's finals weekend fixture at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium and the start of his side's Rugby Championship campaign next summer.

Erasmus said that 17 hip-drop or knee-drop tackles had been missed in South Africa's 21-19 defeat in France by match officials. Andrea Piardi was the referee for the Stade de France fixture, while Matteo Liperini was the TMO.

Erasmus added that if TMOs were not intervening for reviews to limit the number of interruptions during a match then it was "manipulation", before he added that his comments were "not an accusation".

"I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" Erasmus added.

"If the TMO didn't see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result or injured players getting injured.

"So all I'm asking, don't take TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."

In a statement on Tuesday, World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments had met "the threshold for serious misconduct".

World Rugby confirmed the ban will stop Erasmus having any match day involvement for six matches, which includes coaching, direct or indirect contact with the team management or players on match days, entering the stadium, coaches' box, playing enclosure or technical area.

"The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials," its statement said.

"In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity.

"Therefore, the panel reviewed a number of elements of the commentary including the timing and reach of the statements, combined with the allegations of bias or bad faith, and found that the comments attracted a six-match automatic suspension."

World Rugby added that "respect is fundamental to rugby, and match officials are central to the sport".

"Protecting their wellbeing and integrity, and their right to perform without abuse or intimidation, is a responsibility World Rugby and unions take seriously," their statement added.

"Coaches, players, unions and everyone in the game must uphold these standards.

"Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches. Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."

In the same news conference, which lasted more than half an hour at the Springboks' team hotel, Erasmus also questioned what he felt were double standards in terms of sanctions.

The outcome of the citing has yet to be released, but he predicted that Prendergast will be available to play against South Africa due to a "technicality", and also questioned the decision not to ban Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong for an alleged groin grab while playing for Leinster ahead of the November Tests.

Last year, South Africa prop Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-match ban for a similar offence and missed November's matches for the Springboks.

title: Disciplinary update: Rassie Erasmus (South Africa)
article_text:
South Africa men’s 15s head coach Rassie Erasmus has been suspended for six international matches with immediate effect. The sanction follows a review of wide-ranging comments made by Erasmus at a media conference this week concerning officiating during the Springboks’ Nations Championship match against France last Friday.

An independent panel imposed the sanction under World Rugby’s Match Official Abuse Sanction Process. Introduced in July 2026 with national member unions, competitions, International Rugby Match Officials (IRMO) and International Rugby Players’ Association (IRPA) support, the process runs in parallel with Regulation 18 and provides a clear, consistent framework for addressing public criticism of match officials, particularly comments that may undermine the integrity of individuals or the sport, or fuel online abuse.

In line with the process, the panel applied the Match Official Abuse decision making matrix. This is an objective test and assesses the comments against a defined list of characteristics. The outcome of that assessment determines the appropriate outcome, which ranges from no further action up to an automatic suspension.

Having considered the comments which related to the match TMO, the standing Match Official Abuse committee*, chaired by senior officer Adam Casselden SC (Australia) determined that the threshold for serious misconduct had been met. The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials.

In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity. Therefore, the panel reviewed a number of elements of the commentary including the timing and reach of the statements, combined with the allegations of bias or bad faith, and found that the comments attracted a six-match automatic suspension.

The suspension applies with immediate effect, applies to international matches, and includes any match-day involvement including coaching, direct or indirect contact with team management or players on match days; entering the stadium, coaches’ box, playing enclosure, technical area, approaching and/or communicating with match officials on match day; engaging in any ‘feedback’ process with match officials; and engaging in media duties during the suspension.

Respect is fundamental to rugby, and match officials are central to the sport. Protecting their wellbeing and integrity, and their right to perform without abuse or intimidation, is a responsibility World Rugby and unions take seriously. Coaches, players, unions and everyone in the game must uphold these standards.

Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches. Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official’s integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse.

Erasmus is entitled to have the matter referred to a full misconduct hearing.

* The disciplinary panel is appointed in advance of the international window to preside over all cases that arise from the respective competitions in the window.

title: Wales hero poised to leave squad at any moment as 'family comes first'
article_text:
Wales say they will do what is right for James Botham, with the back-row's emotional week set to continue in the coming days.

The back-row was at the heart of Wales' historic victory over New Zealand on Saturday, with the 28-year-old breaking down in tears after his mesmeric player of the match performance. However, it's not just a big week for Botham on the field.

Off it, he's set to become a dad for the first time this week - with Wales insisting he is ready to "shoot off" from camp whenever the time comes.

Having parked the celebrations, attention has turned to facing Australia this weekend - with attack coach Matt Sherratt keen to back up Saturday's win with a similar performance against the Wallabies.

Despite the monumental effort from Wales' players in the All Blacks victory, Sherratt added that all had come through fairly unscathed - with Steve Tandy having essentially a full squad to pick from this week following Tuesday's training session.

"I think we've got a pretty clean bill of health in terms of who is available for selection," said Sherratt, before adding on Botham. "It's just doing what's right for Jim, really.

"Obviously there was a big physical demand for all the players. There was 348 tackles, which is almost two games' worth in one game.

"We're very mindful of that. With Jim, family comes first. We're just making sure he's in contact with home so he can shoot off whenever that may be."

Sherratt confirmed that No. 8 Aaron Wainwright took part in training on Tuesday, although second-row Adam Beard was not involved after a slight shoulder injury.

He is expected to take part in training on Wednesday, though.

Sherratt also elaborated on the impact of Botham, having coached him at Cardiff.

"Do you know what I always think with Jim? Perhaps it's in the surname," said Sherratt.

"He does come to the party when there's a big game. Even at Cardiff, if there's semi-finals or derbies, Jim likes the big occasion.

"I had a bit of a feeling - we all did as a coaching staff - that it was a game for Jim. He's a very good athlete.

"Obviously New Zealand are blessed with athletes. I thought both sides of the ball, Jim was brilliant.

"Obviously his hold-up tackles and his defensive work come to the fore. But his timing in attack, the way he ran onto the ball.

"Probably the things that people don't see. He made a gap for Jac Morgan by timing a short ball off Tomos.

"Little soft skills in attack were really good. I'm really chuffed for Jim. It was great to see him afterwards and how emotional he was."

title: Nadine Roos Back as Bok Women’s Sevens Prepare for SVNS 2
article_text:
The smiles on the faces of the Springbok Women’s Sevens team doctor, Minjon Ras, and long-serving physiotherapist, Reagan Cele, were there for all to see as the squad started preparations for the HSBC SVNS 2 series, set to start in January next year, at training sessions on Monday, 16 November and Tuesday, 17 November 2026.

The reason for their happiness could be explained by the presence of a significant number of players who are back from long-term injuries. They include Nadine Roos, Rights Mkhari, Liske Lategan, Leigh Fortuin, Shannon-Lee Windvogel and Kemisetso Baloyi.

For Ras, seeing these players back running freely was liberating in many ways, as she was often the one who had to relay the results of a scan or booking of a medical procedure.

“As a team doctor, one of the hardest parts of my job is sitting down with a player to break the news of a long-term injury,” said Ras as Cecil Afrika (head coach) and Obakeng Molopyane (S&C coach) took the team through their early-season paces.

“One of the best is getting to celebrate with her when she runs back onto the field alongside her teammates after months of hard work and sacrifice.”

The HSBC SVNS 2 tournaments are set for Nairobi (23 to 24 January), Montevideo (20 to 21 February) and São Paulo (27 to 28 February), and all the focus is on the Kenyan leg for now.

Ras said it is very satisfying to see all the athletes back to training: “As a medical and rehabilitation team, we’re privileged to work with players who push boundaries and do everything they can to get back to the game they love ahead of schedule.

“Sometimes we have to rein in that eagerness, and sometimes they surprise us. What I admire most is how they trust the rehab process and respect the timeframes we set for them.”

Roos, whose injury in Montevideo in March meant she missed most of the season, said the early days were tough, but that she received a lot of support and assistance, both mentally and physically.

“That was my first very serious injury, but I made peace with the injury early on,” said Roos, the SA Rugby Women’s Player of the Year for 2025.

“I realised that it would take a certain amount of time and managing the recovery was key. Returning to the field with the sevens squad – where my career started – was also a full circle moment for me.”

Baloyi, a versatile forward who missed the entire 2026 season, said she found some solace in her studies: “As I was doing my rehab, I used the opportunity provided by Stadio to further my studies and I am currently busy with an LLB.

“That is going well as Stadio’s schedule is responsive to training programmes, but also because of me being back on the training field. It was tough doing rehab while the rest of the squad were running around playing sevens. But now I am running around with them again and that is a great feeling.”

Main Photo Caption: Springbok Women’s Sevens players Nadine Roos, Rights Mkhari, Liske Lategan, Leigh Fortuin, Shannon-Lee Windvogel and Kemisetso Baloyi are back in training after long-term injuries as the squad opens its build-up to the HSBC SVNS 2 series, starting in Nairobi in January 2027. All Photos: SA Rugby / Gallo Images

Photo 2 Caption: Team doctor Minjon Ras and physiotherapist Reagan Cele guided the rehabilitation that has returned six players to the Springbok Women’s Sevens.

title: England stars to help launch Moody MND challenge at All Blacks match
article_text:
Lewis Moody says he has been buoyed by the England team's support as he launches his latest challenge in aid of Motor Neurone Disease (MND) research at Saturday's match against New Zealand at Allianz Stadium.

England will wear training tops and specially-painted boots publicising Moody's 'Front Up' campaign, which is calling on supporters to converge on the British coastline in June for a day of fundraising walks.

"I just couldn't be more grateful to the team, the lads that have been in touch and the energy and excitement they have wanted to bring to this," said Moody.

"To have their buy-in is wonderful for me. It speaks to the connection the rugby family has, whatever the team, the era, the nationality, and the strength of that bond."

Moody, who won 71 England caps, was part of the 2003 Rugby World Cup-winning side and captained the team at the 2011 tournament. He was diagnosed with MND last year.

The muscle-wasting condition impacted the lives of Doddie Weir, the former Scotland and British and Irish Lions second row, and rugby league star Rob Burrow in recent years. Both have since died.

England assistant coach Kevin Sinfield, a friend and former team-mate of Burrow's, has raised more than £13m for the cause through a series of distance-running challenges.

"He's been there from the start for me, on the phone as someone to lean on," said Moody.

"I can't speak highly enough about him as an individual."

Moody, who took part in a 500-mile bike ride in June, is working with Weir's My Name'5 Doddie Foundation again on his latest challenge.

There are 175 routes, each 26 miles long, in England, Scotland and Wales. Participants can walk on 12 June, Moody's birthday. Moody himself is planning to take part either in Cornwall or on a leg in Scotland. The aim is to raise more than £1m for research into MND.

"I'm doing OK, progression remains slow for me," said Moody of his own condition.

"Everyone's journey is slightly different. The harsh stats are 50% are gone within two to three years [of diagnosis] but that means 50% aren't. I remain positive with that, as do my family. I am in a good spot at the minute."

Moody, who alongside his wife Annie has also raised more than £2.5m for research into brain tumours after meeting a terminally ill teenager,, external says he is proudest of how his family have dealt with his diagnosis.

Lewis and Annie have two teenage sons, Dylan and Ethan. Dylan is a professional goalkeeper, who made his England under-19 debut on Wednesday., external

"The thing I am absolutely proudest of is the conversations I have had with my boys and how they've dealt with it," said Lewis.

"There's nothing more important than family. And you never know how you'll deal with something like this.

"But to see how my boys and Annie have coped with this is definitely the thing that I'm proudest of, without a shadow of a doubt. They approach it with the same energy and positivity as me, if not more so."

title: Scotland lose injured quartet for Japan finale
article_text:
Captain Sione Tuipulotu, Ben White, Jack Dempsey and Scott Cummings have all been ruled out of Scotland's final Nations Championship group game at home to Japan on Saturday.

Glasgow Warriors centre Tuipulotu was a late withdrawal from Sunday's win over Australia with a knee injury.

Toulon scrum-half White picked up a knee injury during the game at Murrayfield, with Toshiba Brave Lupus number eight Dempsey injuring a foot and Glasgow lock Cummings picking up leg damage.

Also returning to their clubs through injury after sitting out that game are Saracens back Fergus Burke and Glasgow lock Alex Craig, while Edinburgh prop Ollie Blyth-Lafferty has been released from the squad.

Edinburgh forwards Grant Gilchrist and Magnus Bradbury and Leicester Tigers lock Cam Henderson have, meanwhile, been added to Gregor Townsend's squad.

Ali Price trained with the squad before the Australia game and the Montpellier scrum-half retains his position.

Uncapped Josh McKay qualifies for Scotland on residency grounds this week and the back, who joined Glasgow in 2021, could make his debut against Japan at Murrayfield.

Scotland sit fourth in the Northern Hemisphere table after five matches and the weekend's set of fixtures will determine who their opponents will be when the Nations Championship Finals take place at Allianz Stadium.

Ewan Ashman (Edinburgh), Josh Bayliss (Bath), Magnus Bradbury (Edinburgh), Gregor Brown (Glasgow Warriors), Rory Darge, captain (Glasgow Warriors), Freddy Douglas (Edinburgh), Matt Fagerson (Glasgow Warriors), Zander Fagerson (Glasgow Warriors), Grant Gilchrist (Edinburgh), Jonny Gray (Perpignan), Cam Henderson (Leicester Tigers), Gregor Hiddleston (Glasgow Warriors), Will Hurd (Leicester Tigers), Ollie Leatherbarrow (Newcastle Red Bulls), Nathan McBeth (Glasgow Warriors), Liam McConnell (Edinburgh Rugby), D'arcy Rae (Edinburgh), Pierre Schoeman (Edinburgh), Rory Sutherland (Glasgow Warriors), Seb Stephen (Glasgow Warriors), Max Williamson (Glasgow Warriors).

Jamie Dobie (Glasgow Warriors), Darcy Graham (Edinburgh Rugby), George Horne (Glasgow Warriors), Rory Hutchinson (Northampton Saints), Huw Jones (Toulon), Tom Jordan (Bristol Bears), Blair Kinghorn (Toulouse), Stafford McDowall (Glasgow Warriors), Josh McKay (Glasgow Warriors), Ali Price (Montpellier), Kyle Rowe (Glasgow Warriors), Finn Russell (Bath), Ollie Smith (Glasgow Warriors), Kyle Steyn (Glasgow Warriors), Duhan van der Merwe (Edinburgh).

title: 10 changes to Scotland squad in major update ahead of Japan Nations Championship tie
article_text:
Seven players, including Sione Tuipulotu, have left the Scotland squad ahead of the Nations Championship match against Japan.

Tuipulotu was a late withdrawal from the squad to face Australia on Sunday after aggravating a knee problem he picked up against New Zealand.

Scott Cummings, meanwhile, limped out of the weekend win after 25 minutes after injuring his leg after landing awkwardly from a lineout.

Scrum-half Ben White started both games but had his left leg heavily strapped and received attention on several occasions against Australia before making way for Jamie Dobie early in the second half.

Dempsey, meanwhile, picked up a knee injury against the country of his birth.

And squad members Fergus Burke and Alex Craig, who did not feature in either of the first two matches, have also left the squad with leg injuries.

The wait also goes on to see Ollie Blyth-Lafferty in Test rugby. The 20-year-old Edinburgh prospect has also been released back to the capital club, but not due to an injury.

Edinburgh Rugby’s Grant Gilchrist and Magnus Bradbury join Townsend's squad with Leicester Tigers’ Cam Henderson also involved in the squad switch-up.

Ali Price trained with the squad before the Australia game before returning to Montpellier, but the 33-year-old scrum-half is now back with the Scotland squad once more.

He could be in line for a first cap in two years if selected this weekend.

title: Scotland lose trio of Lions for remainder of Nations Championship
article_text:
Scotland captain Sione Tuipulotu and fellow British and Irish Lions tourists Ben White and Scott Cummings have returned to their respective clubs after picking up Nations Championship-ending injuries.

Tuipulotu was ruled out of Sunday’s 15-12 victory over Australia at the eleventh hour with a knee injury, while Cummings (thigh) was replaced by Max Williamson midway through the first half and Ben White (knee) lasted 10 minutes of the second half before Jamie Dobie took on the scrum-half duties.

Number eight Jack Dempsey is also named on the six-man injury list announced by the Scottish Rugby Union, having suffered a foot injury against his former team, while fly-half Fergus Burke and lock Alex Craig, who both have leg injuries, have also been ruled out of the remainder of the Nations Championship. In addition, prop Ollie Blyth-Lafferty has returned to his club.

Veteran Edinburgh lock Grant Gilchrist and Leicester Tigers’ Cam Henderson have been added to the second-row options alongside Gregor Brown, Jonny Gray and Williamson, who made a telling impact off the bench at Murrayfield.

A third addition sees Edinburgh No.8 Magnus Bradbury replace Dempsey, joining the back-row stocks which include captain at the weekend Rory Darge, Josh Bayliss, Matt Fagerson, recent debutant Ollie Leatherbarrow plus Liam McConnell and Freddy Douglas.

In the front row, all three loosehead props (Pierre Schoeman, Rory Sutherland and Nathan McBeth) and hookers (Seb Stephen, Ewan Ashman and Gregor Hiddleston) are retained. D’arcy Rae has returned to the squad since the initial announcement, joining Zander Fagerson and Will Hurd as options at tighthead.

Experienced Montpellier scrum-half Ali Price, who won the last of his 67 caps against Fiji in November 2024, trained with the squad ahead of the Australia game and has retained his position alongside Jamie Dobie and George Horne. Finn Russell and Tom Jordan remain as the fly-half options.

Huw Jones, Rory Hutchinson and Stafford McDowall are options in midfield, with a versatile set of back-three players available, featuring Darcy Graham, Blair Kinghorn, Kyle Rowe, Kyle Steyn, Duhan van der Merwe, Josh McKay and Ollie Smith.

The uncapped McKay qualifies for Scotland on residency grounds this week, having joined Glasgow Warriors in 2021.

Scotland face Japan at Murrayfield on Saturday and will then contest one of the play-off matches at the Nations Championship Finals weekend at the Allianz Stadium, Twickenham from 27-29 November.

Fixtures determined by the placings of the northern and southern hemisphere countries after the six matches across July and November, with Scotland currently sitting in fourth in the northern standings.

title: Rassie Erasmus: World Rugby could review South Africa head coach's extraordinary comments about double standards from officials
article_text:
World Rugby could review Rassie Erasmus' comments after the Springboks head coach made a string of extraordinary claims regarding officiating and decisions going against his side.

Not for the first time, Erasmus delivered a strikingly outspoken press conference on Monday, suggesting officials missed 17 illegal tackles against his side in their narrow loss to France, going as far as to question whether "manipulation" of the result is behind why incidents such as these are not picked up by officials during matches.

He also predicted that a "technicality" will emerge that sees Ireland's Sam Prendergast free to play Saturday's game against South Africa, after the fly-half was cited for a hip-drop tackle in his side's win over Fiji last weekend.

World Rugby could review Erasmus' comments in the context of the match official abuse sanction framework that was introduced earlier this year.

That process was brought in to reduce comments that lead to "the unacceptable increase in abuse and threats towards match officials".

Under this framework, an independent three-person panel review the comments to determine if they were made with a view to undermining confidence in officials, with potential punishments including multiple match bans.

Erasmus has found himself in hot water for publicly admonishing the performances of officials in the past. In 2021, he was banned from all rugby activity for two months for his behaviour towards match officials during his side's Test series against the British and Irish Lions, during which he released an hour-long video critiquing the referee's display in the first Test.

On Monday, Erasmus questioned why many of France's knee-drop tackles he believed to be illegal were not reviewed by the video referee.

"Let's say 11 of those were at least a penalty and three I thought was at least three yellow cards. And not one was sanctioned and not one was showed out or cited," Erasmus said in widely-reported quotes.

"I'll send you the playlist but I'll get into trouble… So I can't send the playlist to anybody and we can only send five clips to World Rugby. So we'll probably query it but the answer will probably be: 'Yes, it was a mistake, it should have been penalised'.

"On numerous times we mentioned to the referee 'we think there's a knee-drop tackle'. I'm saying to you my feeling is that knee-drop tackles is out. They happened 17 times in our game. Not one was penalised."

"And if the TMO didn't see it, then maybe technology must be better. If he saw it and ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result? Or players getting injured?

"So, all I'm asking is don't take the TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."

It is not yet known if Ireland fly-half Prendergast will be available for Saturday's crunch Nations Championship meeting at Dublin's Aviva Stadium, after he was cited for an alleged illegal hip-drop tackle against Fiji.

Despite the lack of ruling, Erasmus made it clear that he does not expect Prendergast to be penalised.

"We are in the northern hemisphere," Erasmus said. "I think there is going to be a technicality and he is going to play.

"We all thought it's an immediate red card. Everybody watched the game live because that's exactly what they said the hip-drop tackle is," he said.

"I swear I'm not moaning. I'm just trying to give you a perspective of somebody who comes and plays, for example, in France or in Ireland."

Ireland and South Africa have enjoyed an intense and at times fraught rivalry in recent years, with Ireland head coach Andy Farrell winning three of his five meetings against the Springboks.

However, South Africa were victorious in the most recent chapter of the rivalry, winning in Dublin a year ago in a game which saw five Irish players carded.

Should he be available, Prendergast would be expected to start at No 10 on Saturday, something Erasmus believes would not be fair given his tackle last weekend.

"It's difficult to understand when the TMO sits there and he sees that," he said.

"And it was something we discussed at the World Rugby meeting, and the examples of how it is was shown over and over, and we all had input.

"Somebody sees that and he decides there's nothing wrong with that."

title: World Rugby launch investigation into Springboks after wild 'match-fixing' rant
article_text:
World Rugby are set to investigate extraordinary comments made by South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus, who posed a question about "match-fixing and manipulation" taking place during their defeat to France last Friday.

The outspoken Springboks boss questioned whether World Rugby match officials who witness foul play but fail to intervene could be influencing the outcome of matches, following his side's defeat to France on Friday night.

Erasmus claimed there were as many as 17 knee-drop tackles committed against his players during the contest in Paris, none of which resulted in a sanction. He also questioned the handling of an incident involving Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast against Fiji.

According to Sky Sports the 54-year-old's comments at Monday's astonishing press conference will now be investigated by World Rugby, which could potentially lead to a ban.

The comments are being reviewed under World Rugby's match official abuse sanction framework, which was introduced earlier this year in response to an "unacceptable increase in abuse and threats towards match officials".

An independent three-person panel will assess whether Erasmus' remarks were intended to undermine confidence in match officials. If found guilty, he could face a range of sanctions, including a lengthy match ban.

This is not the first time the double Rugby World Cup-winning coach has been in hot water with World Rugby.

During the 2021 British & Irish Lions tour of South Africa he was banned from all rugby activities for two months after releasing an hour-long video critiquing the referee's performance in the first Test.

Speaking to reporters in Dublin on Monday, Erasmus said: "I'm not saying he's wrong, I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing? Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game if you see this injury that happened there, a knee-drop tackle happened there, and it's been decided that knee drop tackles are out?"

He continued: "Now, I'm saying to you, my feeling is knee drop tackles is out. They happened 17 in our games. Not one was penalised even.

"And if the TMO didn't see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to?

"Manipulation of the game or the result or injured players getting injured. So all I'm asking, don't take TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."

When it was put to Erasmus that he was making a serious insinuation, the South African immediately insisted he was not accusing anyone of wrongdoing.

"It's not an accusation, it's not an accusation," he replied.

He claimed his analysis of the France defeat had identified 17 knee-drop tackles, of which he believed 11 warranted at least a penalty and three deserved yellow cards.

"Let's say 11 of those were, I thought, at least a penalty and three I thought were at least yellow card," he said. "And not one was sanctioned. And not one was showed out or cited."

South Africa face Ireland in Dublin in the final round robin clash of the Nations Championship.
